extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors learning or teaching foundations of algebraic geometry (first serious year-level)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and conventions for a rigorous yet approachable first-year graduate (or serious self-study) textbook on the foundations of algebraic geometry, covering core topics with examples, exercises, and minimal prerequisites. Emphasizes what to include, omit, and how to present material pedagogically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasiseparatedness as standard hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce and use the notion of quasiseparatedness early and often; accept the extra vocabulary cost because essentially every scheme of interest is quasiseparated and the hypothesis 'quasicompact and quasiseparated' signals key proof ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the term and habitually use it in statements so readers will immediately guess proof ideas when the phrase appears. Treat the one extra word as worthwhile for clarity in proofs and statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish coherent vs finite-type (quasicoherent) sheaves
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when coherent and finite type quasicoherent sheaves coincide in Noetherian situations, keep the distinction in statements and exercises to be explicit about what hypotheses the proofs use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State which notion is used in a proof or exercise so the reader understands the precise assumptions; avoid conflating concepts merely because they agree in special cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about omitted topics
rubrics_metrics.description: State which important topics are intentionally not covered (e.g., valuative criteria, dévissage, formal schemes, cohomology with supports) and relegate some statements to optional sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly label omissions and optional material so instructors and readers know what the book does not attempt, and so they can supplement as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: State foundational and algebraic conventions up front
rubrics_metrics.description: Set concrete conventions early: all rings commutative (unless noted), rings contain unit and maps send 1 to 1, allow the 0-ring, define notation for local rings (A, m) or (A, m, k), etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make these conventions explicit to avoid ambiguity in later chapters; note any nonstandard but deliberate choices (e.g., allowing the 0-ring).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept (and state) set-theoretic choices like the Axiom of Choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare acceptance of the Axiom of Choice and note where it is used (for instance, any proper ideal lies in a maximal ideal; existence of enough injectives in module categories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alert readers to where nonconstructive principles are invoked and provide references for those who wish to avoid them.

rubrics_metrics.name: List prerequisite background clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the reader what elementary commutative algebra and related material is assumed: ideals (prime/maximal), types of rings (domains, PIDs, UFDs, local rings), localization, modules, tensor products, exact sequences, structure theorem for f.g. modules over a PID, and some field theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State which prerequisites are essential and which are merely helpful; indicate where brief development is given in the book versus where external references are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about delicate foundational issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly avoid getting into subtle set-theoretic or universe-level foundational issues, while naming references for readers who need that level of care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell readers you will avoid these issues for exposition but point them to sources (e.g., [KS2, 1.1]) if they must attend to foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommend supplementary references for background
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggest companion texts for dipping into specific facts: e.g., [E] for commutative algebra, [AtM], [Mat2], [Al] for algebraic geometry viewpoints, [Weib] for homological algebra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage readers to have such books at hand for facts they do not wish to learn in advance; name recommended works by topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare nonmathematical word usage and optional sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain idiosyncratic uses of words (e.g., 'unimportant' means 'unimportant for the current exposition') and mark optional material with stars: ⋆ for sections useful on a second reading, ⋆⋆ for sections to avoid on a first reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent marking and explain reading priority: do not read double-starred sections unless you really want to; starred sections are optional but valuable later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary goal: cover a canon completely and rigorously with examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to cover a canonical core of the subject completely and rigorously, supplying enough examples and calculations to develop intuition for the machinery; treat this as a first (but challenging) introduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on a conservative canon that most algebraic geometers agree on; be selective about extras and prepare the reader for a demanding but coherent year-long course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-contained development: 'if you use it, you must prove it'
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the motto that whenever the book uses a fact, it should provide a proof (or a quick development) rather than deferring indefinitely to external sources, to reduce prerequisites for readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that this makes the book denser and demands more maturity, but results in more accessible exposition for readers who lack background; explicitly develop facts 'quickly from scratch' when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises are central to learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Make exercises a core part of the book's pedagogy; they are essential for building intuition and practical facility with the machinery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design exercises to reinforce theoretical points and develop examples; indicate which are important for mastery (see 0.0.1 reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the book usable both for courses and self-study
rubrics_metrics.description: Write material so it can be adapted to a course (instructor personality will shape coverage) and so motivated self-learners can use it, though group/contact with others is recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize content modularly so instructors can choose which 'inessential' topics to include; advise self-learners to read in groups or have someone to ask questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize prerequisites while demanding intellectual maturity
rubrics_metrics.description: Require in a technical sense minimal background (ideally just some commutative algebra and point-set topology) but be explicit that the book is not light and expects readers to work hard and bring maturity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be honest about the effort required: the less background a reader has, the harder they will need to work; indicate what can be learned on the fly in the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build intuition via examples and categorical thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize examples, calculations, and categorical viewpoints (e.g., universal properties) to build intuition for abstract machinery; motivate definitions by revisiting familiar cases (sets, manifolds) first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce universal properties early (products, initial/final objects, localization) and use them to argue uniqueness up to unique isomorphism; transition from concrete examples to abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer universal-property and conceptual proofs when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor arguments based on universal properties and categorical reasoning over messy explicit constructions when these give clearer, more general insights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit constructions for intuition but present universal-property arguments to show why objects are canonical and to simplify proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope focus: do not attempt encyclopedic coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentionally avoid being encyclopedic (e.g., largely ignore analytic aspects) and make hard editorial choices to focus on algebraic foundations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State plainly what the book will not attempt and keep the scope narrow enough to be tractable within the stated goals (e.g., digestible core in a year).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical progression: start from known things
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by telling readers things they already know, describe essential features of examples, then abstract a definition and show it in less familiar settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This progression helps readers accept abstractions; for instance, motivate product of schemes by revisiting product in Sets and manifolds before giving categorical definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make notation and presentation choices explicit and consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Define notation (e.g., localization Af, Ap, local ring notation) and warn about potential confusions (e.g., Af vs Ap when (f) is prime), and present constructive definitions alongside universal ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag notational warnings and provide both concrete constructions and universal-property reinterpretations so readers understand both computational and conceptual viewpoints.
